title: Conformity Cases for Learning-Enabled Robots
one_liner: A compliance workbench and pre-assessment service that builds the CE-marking safety case for machines whose behaviour comes from ML models (warehouse robots, cobots, humanoids) ahead of the new EU Machinery Regulation.
customer: CTOs and safety engineers at robotics startups and integrators (10-300 staff) selling autonomous mobile robots, cobot cells, agri-robots, humanoids and exoskeletons into the EU.
problem: The Machinery Regulation applies from 20 Jan 2027 and adds duties for machinery with self-evolving or learning behaviour and for cybersecurity (background, verify), with AI Act Annex I overlay dated 2 Aug 2028 in the tracker. Consultancies know ISO 12100 and 13849 but not how to argue the safety of a neural-network policy, notified bodies have no playbook, and startups cannot sell to EU customers without a CE dossier.
solution: Software plus an expert network: hazard-analysis templates for ML perception and control, runtime safety-monitor patterns (shielding, safe fallback, speed and separation monitoring), test evidence generated from simulation and field logs, and a traceable assurance case linking hazards to mitigations to evidence, mapped to Machinery, CRA and AI Act. A partner notified body does a pre-review.
why_now: Foundation-model-controlled and humanoid robots reached commercial pilots in 2025-26, and the regulatory dates arrive within months. Assurance-case methods from aviation and automated driving are mature but have not reached robotics.
revenue_model: EUR 25-80k per product safety-case project, $2-6k/month SaaS, and notified-body referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The blocker for deploying humanoids in Europe is not the model but an argument a regulator can accept. The first team whose safety cases are accepted creates precedent that competitors must copy, which is a durable moat.
first_30_days: Interview 20 robotics startups and publish an 'ML robot CE checklist'. Sign three design partners at EUR 10-15k for a gap analysis and recruit an ex-notified-body functional-safety engineer as co-founder or advisor.

title: Idle Brewery Tanks as Biotech Pilot Plants
one_liner: Retrofit closing or underused craft breweries into shared 200 to 2,000 liter fermentation pilot plants for food-ingredient, cosmetic-ingredient and biomaterial startups.
customer: Pre-seed to Series A synthetic-biology and food-tech startups that need samples, regulatory batches and customer trials at pilot scale, plus struggling brewery owners who get rent or revenue share.
problem: Startups can make grams in the lab but face a valley before contract manufacturers will touch them: schedules booked, minimums high, and building their own plant is slow. Pilot-scale fermentation capacity is a widely reported gap. Meanwhile craft brewers are closing: 481 closures against 300 openings in 2025, and 9,344 breweries operating in June 2026, down 1.8% year over year.
solution: A 'bio-foundry co-op'. Lease off-hours tank time from 1 to 3 breweries. Add a portable sterile-air skid, in-place cleaning and sterilization protocols, a single-use inoculum train, and harvest and dewatering equipment (decanter or centrifuge, with drying done through mobile partners). Start with well-characterized yeast (Saccharomyces, Pichia) and other low-risk hosts. Sell fixed-price run packages, with brewer-trained operators supervised by a process scientist.
why_now: Breweries are stranded with stainless tanks, utilities, trade-waste permits and skilled operators, while beer volume keeps shrinking. Food and materials biotech has more strains than pilot capacity. The gap is at 500 to 2,000 liters, not 100,000, and that is exactly brewery scale.
revenue_model: Per-run fees ($8k to $25k), tech-transfer and process-development fees, a rent or revenue share to the brewery, and later a multi-year reserved-capacity subscription for repeat customers.
non_obvious_insight: The moat isn't the tank, it's the permitting: zoning, industrial wastewater discharge capacity for high-BOD effluent, food-grade utilities and a building already approved for fermentation take biotech companies years to secure. Breweries have all of it. Brewers are also the biggest pool of people who instinctively know how to keep yeast at scale contamination-free.
first_30_days: Sign a letter of intent with one distressed brewery on an off-hours share. Recruit 3 startups from synbio and food-tech directories and sell a paid $5k to $10k feasibility run at 200 liters. Prepare a biosafety plan and speak to the local wastewater authority early. Line up a part-time process scientist.

title: PFAS Turf Audits and Replacement Planning
one_liner: Field-by-field PFAS and regulatory risk audits plus replacement bid packages for school districts and parks departments with aging synthetic turf.
customer: School district facilities directors, athletic directors, municipal parks and recreation departments and colleges.
problem: Thousands of synthetic fields installed in the 2010s are reaching end of life just as PFAS rules bite: New York's ban on selling PFAS-containing turf takes effect December 31, 2026, California's restriction on PFAS in covered surfaces began January 1, 2026, and other states (New Jersey, Maine) have bills to pause purchases. Districts do not know what is under their fields, may not be able to buy what they always bought, and face bond votes and parent pressure.
solution: A $2.5-8k audit per district: field inventory (age, product, manufacturer), lab testing of fibers and infill through an accredited partner, legal exposure summary, lifecycle-cost comparison of synthetic, PFAS-free, hybrid and natural grass, and turnkey bid documents; then project-management and referral fees.
why_now: 2026 effective dates, active parent and environmental groups, and pending state bills create urgent, budgeted decisions.
revenue_model: $2.5-8k audits, testing pass-through margin, 2-4 percent project-management fees on $500k-1.5M projects, supplier referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody owns 'what is my turf made of' data and manufacturers will not volunteer it. Sitting between district, lab and contractor makes you the neutral spec writer who controls the RFP.
first_30_days: Build a public-records inventory of turf fields in New York from bond documents and board minutes, pitch 50 districts, line up an accredited lab, and sell three audits.

title: Compliance-as-Code for EWA and BNPL
one_liner: State-by-state earned wage access and BNPL rules are being written fast. Turn them into an API that checks fees, tips and disclosures before each product release.
customer: EWA and BNPL providers, payroll platforms and neobanks adding these features, and employers running EWA programs.
problem: Colorado sued EarnIn (2026-09-08), Maryland banned EWA tipping, and New York and Illinois have BNPL rules. Each state differs on fees, tips, disclosures and licensing. Product managers ship copy and fee configs faster than lawyers can review them.
solution: A rules engine and configuration API. Providers submit product configs (fees, tip prompts, speed, limits) and get per-state pass/fail, required disclosure text, and a change log. It also monitors new bills and enforcement actions and produces exam-ready evidence.
why_now: Enforcement began in Sept 2026 and legislatures are still moving. Providers need pre-release checks now and will need audit trails when examiners arrive.
revenue_model: $3k-$10k per month per provider, with per-state add-ons and content licensing to law firms.
non_obvious_insight: EWA's legal risk sits in UI copy and fee configuration, which product teams change weekly. Rules-as-code plugs into release management, which a law-firm memo never can.
first_30_days: Publish a free 12-state EWA and BNPL rule tracker as a lead magnet. Pair with a fintech law firm and pitch five mid-size providers and payroll platforms on a $3k per month pilot.

title: Independent Robot Bake-Off and Acceptance Lab
one_liner: A neutral test cell where warehouse buyers watch robots handle their own SKUs and pallets before signing, with published, verified throughput numbers.
customer: Mid-size 3PLs, grocers and retailers (roughly 50-500k sq ft) evaluating palletizing, picking or humanoid pilots. Robot vendors are a second payer (for certification), and lenders and insurers are a third.
problem: Vendors control the demo. Buyers cannot verify throughput on their own product mix, and pilots eat 6-12 months. Funding is running far ahead of proof: Maven raised a $100M Series A with about 8 robots deployed, Agility booked $1.8M of revenue against a $2.5B SPAC valuation, and early 1X NEO demos were largely teleoperated.
solution: Rent a 20-30k sq ft cell in a logistics hub. Buyers ship 200 pallets or 500 SKUs. Vendors run their robots under a standard protocol. The lab logs picks per hour, error rate, human-intervention minutes, teleop minutes and mean time between failures, then issues a 'Verified Throughput' report. Buyers pay per bake-off, and vendors pay to list certified results and retest after software updates.
why_now: In 2026 procurement teams face a flood of unverifiable claims: about 22k humanoids shipped in H1, nine-figure rounds go to companies with a handful of deployed units, and buyers want outcome pricing. Nobody independent sits between vendors and buyers.
revenue_model: $15-40k per buyer-commissioned bake-off, $25-75k a year per vendor for certification and retests, and data licensing of failure-mode datasets to insurers and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The industry's binding constraint is trust in claims, not capability. Vendors will pay for independent verification because their real bottleneck is a 9-12 month sales cycle (compare UL, J.D. Power, Wirecutter). The failure-mode data becomes an asset that insurers, lenders and model developers all want.
first_30_days: Rent demo floor space inside a friendly integrator's or 3PL's idle mezzanine. Sign 2 mid-size 3PLs to paid bake-offs of 3 vendors each, and give vendors a free first test in exchange for the right to publish. Release the public methodology and a first leaderboard of 'intervention minutes per hour'.

title: Delay Insurance for Data Center Energization
one_liner: Parametric insurance and pricing data that pay developers and lenders when the utility misses its committed energization date.
customer: Data center developers, construction lenders and hyperscale tenants with delivery-date penalties. Reinsurers supply the capital.
problem: A delayed 60 MW site costs about $14M a month. Utilities commit to dates that slip, standard delay-in-start-up cover excludes utility delay, and developers cannot hedge the largest schedule risk in the AI buildout.
solution: Build a database of utility energization performance (committed versus actual dates) by utility and substation type. Write parametric cover with the trigger set at the utility's committed date plus N days, under an MGA or coverholder structure with a Lloyd's or reinsurance backer. Also sell a 'time-to-power index' to lenders and developers.
why_now: The hyperscale pipeline is huge, waits reach years, and new large-load tariffs formalize committed dates, so the risk is finally observable in public filings.
revenue_model: Premium of roughly 2-5% of limit a year, with 15-20% MGA commission, plus data subscriptions from lenders and developers.
non_obvious_insight: Delay looks uninsurable only until you notice it is parametric. The trigger is the utility's own date, which the developer cannot move, and it is currently priced by gut.
first_30_days: Compile a dataset from ~200 public PUC and utility large-load filings. Publish a free 'Time-to-Power Index' teaser. Meet three MGAs or coverholders. Pitch 10 lenders. Land one design-partner letter of intent.

title: Off-Ramp Cohorts for AI-Companion Dependence
one_liner: Eight-week, in-person, non-shaming cohorts that help heavy AI-companion users rebuild human contact, sold to individuals and to employee assistance and counseling providers.
customer: Adults roughly 22-45 who spend two or more hours a day with AI companions (Replika, Character.AI, voice-mode chatbots), plus their worried partners and parents. Second wave: EAP vendors, university counseling centers and behavioral-health plans that have no protocol for this.
problem: Research suggests companions relieve loneliness in small doses but deepen it with heavy daily use; a two-year Aalto study of nearly 2,000 Replika users reportedly found heavy use raised the perceived cost of human relationships and tracked with more depression and loneliness. Lawsuits (Character.AI and Google settled the Garcia case in January 2026) and new laws (California SB 243 in effect since January 1, 2026, Washington HB 2225 signed in March) put the harm on the record, but clinicians have no playbook, users feel judged, and therapy waitlists are long.
solution: A harm-reduction curriculum, not abstinence. Week by week, participants audit what the companion provides (constant availability, validation, safe rehearsal), then re-home each need with a human equivalent: a weekly cohort dinner, a scheduled 'warm call' partner, rehearsal of hard conversations with a facilitator, and a graduated time-box on usage. Ten people per city per cohort, led by trained coaches with a licensed clinician supervising, screening for crisis, and referring out when needed. Pre/post measurement with a validated loneliness scale. Ends with a graduation dinner rather than a discharge.
why_now: Companion apps now have tens of millions of users, the APA flagged AI relationships as a major 2026 trend, and settlements and state laws have made 'what happens to heavy users' a public question. Operators under companion-chatbot laws need credible places to send users, and no incumbent exists. The EU AI Act provisions covering companion-style products are phasing in through 2026.
revenue_model: $395 per seat for an 8-week consumer cohort; $150-250 per seat through EAP and counseling partners; $1,200 curriculum license plus about $30 per participant for therapists and coaches who run their own cohorts; later, outcomes-based contracts with behavioral-health plans.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody pays to 'quit', but people pay to get more out of life, and the winning frame is nicotine-style harm reduction that meets the underlying need (low-stakes rehearsal, non-judgmental availability) with human structures. The competitor is not therapy, it is the AI, so the product has to be as easy to start as opening the app. Companion operators facing liability will eventually want a referral partner, which is a distribution channel nobody has built yet.
first_30_days: Recruit 12 participants from Replika, Character.AI and related communities with a screener asking who would try reducing use. Contract an LPC or clinical psychologist as supervising advisor and write a crisis-referral protocol. Run a 4-week pilot in one city in a cafe or coworking back room, charging $150. Collect pre/post loneliness scores and testimonials, then approach five EAP vendors and three university counseling centers with the data. Keep marketing to coaching and wellness, with no clinical claims.

title: CMMC Enclave for CNC Shops
one_liner: A prebuilt, shop-floor-aware CUI enclave and evidence pack that gets 20-person machine shops through CMMC Level 2 without rebuilding their IT.
customer: Job shops and small manufacturers making parts for defense primes (castings, forgings, machined parts), roughly 30,000-plus firms in the defense supply base.
problem: CMMC Level 2 assessments for contract awards ramp up from Nov 2026 (verify dates). Shops keep CUI drawings on machine-side PCs and USB sticks, and generic CMMC consultants scope the entire company. Sub-tier suppliers lack IT staff and capital, exactly the bottleneck AIA-Bain describes.
solution: A managed enclave that isolates only the CAD/CAM and CNC controllers handling CUI, ships as a pre-configured appliance plus cloud tenant, and comes with policies, evidence collection and assessor liaison. Fixed monthly price, no consultants hourly.
why_now: Phase-in of the CMMC rule puts assessment on contracts through 2026-27, and primes are pushing flow-down requirements. Sub-tier financing is scarce, so shops need a low-capex option.
revenue_model: $800-2,500 per month per shop plus $5-15K onboarding. Channel through primes who will subsidize their suppliers' compliance.
non_obvious_insight: Scope reduction is the whole business. The winning product understands machine tool OT and draws a tight boundary around it, while horizontal CMMC vendors sell a heavy enterprise program.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 shops through a regional manufacturing extension partnership. Assemble the appliance from commodity parts. Sign one prime's supplier program as channel.

title: Sunset Software Co: Pledge-Funded Tool Revival
one_liner: When a B2B tool announces its shutdown, customers pre-commit to paid 'extended life' contracts, and a small operator takes over only if a threshold is met.
customer: Companies stranded when a small dev or data tool shuts down or is acqui-hired away: CI runners, SQL clients, project trackers, metrics services. The founder of the dying tool is the second counterparty and receives a revenue share.
problem: Acqui-hires and product-gap closures strand paying customers with 30-90 days notice. BuildJet closed runners on 31 Mar 2026 because 'GitHub has made substantial improvements.' Cirrus CI closed on 1 Jun 2026 when Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI. Garnix shut down after being acquired. One customer wrote 'I have two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter.' Founders cannot sell the code. An Ask HN founder 'couldn't sell the codebase', and a commenter said 'no one wants some abandoned open source project for a defunct business.' PopSQL, SeekWell and Pivotal Tracker left solo builders racing to fill the gap.
solution: Run a 'continuity pledge' during the notice window. The customer signs a 12-month extended-life contract at 1.2-1.5x the old price, conditional on the operator reaching a minimum pledge total, like a Kickstarter for revival. If the threshold is met, the operator takes a code and brand licence, keeps the service running with a founder retainer or revenue share, and gets paid from day one. If not, nobody pays and nothing is bought. Portfolio economics do the rest: many small tools, shared infrastructure, no CAC.
why_now: AI-lab and platform acqui-hires now regularly turn small devtools into shutdown notices. Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI, Bun joined Anthropic, Astro joined Cloudflare, and Tailwind joined Shopify in the last year. The acquirer wants the team, not the customers. Permissive licences (Cirrus relicensed Tart and related tools as 'more permissive') make forks legal. The SimpleClosure H1 2026 report shows shutdowns running at scale.
revenue_model: 60-80% of extended-life fees kept by the operator, with 20-40% shared with the founder for 12 months. Later, cross-sell hosted plans to the open-source user base.
non_obvious_insight: A dying tool's code has no buyers, but its running service has customers who will pay. The sellable asset is customer continuity, and the pledge threshold removes the risk of buying dead code. Evidence: the Ask HN thread has a founder who could not sell his codebase and a commenter saying no one wants an abandoned project (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44398065). Cirrus CI's closure and Tart relicensing are covered at https://cirruslabs.org/ (HN discussion 47730194, 282 points). The Garnix thread has the 'two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter' comment (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48317043). BuildJet's notice sets the 31 Mar 2026 date (https://buildjet.com/for-github-actions/blog/we-are-shutting-down). Demand for a replacement shows up as solo builders rushing in, for example Saturn SQL after PopSQL and SeekWell (https://saturnsql.com) and the 10 teams racing to replace Pivotal Tracker (https://bye-tracker.net).
first_30_days: Week 1: set up a monitor on HN, status pages and changelogs for shutdown announcements. Week 2: pick one tool currently in its notice window and email the founder with a 12-month revenue-share offer. Weeks 3-4: publish a pledge page for that tool with a fixed pledge threshold and a 21-day deadline. If it clears the threshold, sign the licence and run the tool on shared infrastructure.

title: Show Safe: Compliance and Theft Registry
one_liner: An operating layer for card-show and fan-convention promoters that handles vendor tax permits, insurance certificates, secure check-in and a shared stolen-slab registry.
customer: Promoters of card shows, comic and anime cons (thousands across the US) and vendor associations.
problem: State rules put promoters on the hook for collecting tax on admissions and verifying vendor permits (RI, NY and TX guidance). Armed robberies and thefts of collectors and vendors spiked in 2026 (CNN, April 2026; $100k stolen from a Burbank card store; about $10k stolen at Anime NYC). Promoters run on spreadsheets and Facebook groups.
solution: Vendor onboarding with per-state permit and tax-ID verification and insurance certificate upload, table booking and payments, badge check-in and out logs, incident reporting, and a registry of stolen graded-card cert numbers and serials that vendors and stores can scan-check. Optional admissions-tax filing.
why_now: The 2026 theft wave and insurer scrutiny make promoters want safety and paperwork rigor. The registry's value grows with every show that joins.
revenue_model: $150-500 per show SaaS, ~1.5% on payments, registry API access for stores, and insurance referrals.
non_obvious_insight: Promoters are the choke point where thousands of vendors meet, so the stolen-goods network effect belongs to whoever sees vendor flow. Compliance is the reason to sign up, and the registry is the moat.
first_30_days: Sign 10 local promoters with a free first show. Seed the registry from public theft reports on social media. Charge from show two.

title: Amps Not Acres: Power Headroom for Retrofits
one_liner: Headroom reports and a load-sequencing kit that let plants add machines inside existing walls without a new transformer.
customer: Owners and plant managers of 20-300 employee manufacturers, and machine-tool, compressor and robot dealers who need to know whether a customer can power what they sell.
problem: Site selectors and economic developers think reshoring is limited by land, buildings and permits. The data say otherwise. Factory construction is down 22-32% from peak, yet nondefense capital-goods orders hit a record $85.9B in July, so equipment is going into old buildings. Transformer and switchgear prices are up 89-96% since 2019 as data centers compete for the same gear. Utility service upgrades cost six figures and take a year or more.
solution: Step 1 is a Headroom Report. It pulls 12 months of utility interval data (Green Button) and uses measured demand (NEC 220.87 allows this) to show how many kW can be added, ready for a PE stamp. Step 2 is a clamp-on CT and PLC/gateway kit that staggers compressors, furnaces, welders and spindle start-ups to cap demand peaks. Step 3 adds an optional battery or thermal-storage partner for the residual gap.
why_now: Record capital-goods orders with $953B unfilled, prices for electrical gear up sharply, and reshoring that is happening in existing buildings. No incumbent sells 'create amps in software' to a 50-person shop.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per report (dealers pay to close sales). $5-15k for hardware and install. $200-400 a month for monitoring. Referral fees from dealers and battery vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nameplate capacity is not the constraint. Measured coincident peak is, and it is usually far below service rating. The scarce input is amps, and amps can be created by sequencing loads.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 machine dealers on the report as a free pre-sale add-on. Get interval data from 5 plants. Partner with a licensed PE for stamping. Assemble the first controller from off-the-shelf CTs and a PLC.

title: Workforce Pell Approval-as-a-Service
one_liner: A fixed-fee desk that turns a college's short-program idea into an approved Workforce Pell application with employer-demand evidence, outcomes math and state sign-off.
customer: Community colleges, technical colleges, proprietary trade schools, workforce boards and apprenticeship sponsors with 8-15 week programs (EMT, CDL, welding, medical assistant, phlebotomy).
problem: Workforce Pell launched July 1, 2026 but only 5 programs were approved by September 22. Colleges call the process hard and complicated. They lack capacity to prove employer demand, calculate outcome tests and obtain governor and state workforce-board sign-off, while vocational-heavy public two-years grew 11.7% in Spring 2025.
solution: Done-for-you application packages: a local labor-demand memo with job-posting data and employer letters, cost-versus-earnings math, outcomes tracking setup for completion and placement, and state-by-state approval navigation. Design programs to be apprenticeship-linked, because registered apprenticeships with college instruction auto-qualify as in-demand and up to 49% of instruction can be outsourced to employers or unions.
why_now: The program is three months old, states are still building approval procedures, and the first approvals came from Iowa Central (EMT) and Ivy Tech (medical assistant). First movers get enrollment for the 2027 terms.
revenue_model: $12-30k per program application plus $500-1,500 a month for outcomes reporting; optional success fee.
non_obvious_insight: The constraint is not curriculum or students but making programs legible to regulators. Approval capacity is the scarce resource, so whoever standardizes the evidence package becomes the gatekeeper's best friend.
first_30_days: Read the statute and guidance, and pick two states with active approvals. Offer 3 community colleges a fixed price with a partial success guarantee. Publish a free checklist to pull leads from workforce boards.

title: Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator
one_liner: An advice-only LINE tool that tells franchise convenience-store owners how many fresh items to order and when to mark them down, using the owner's own payoff instead of HQ's.
customer: Franchise convenience-store owners in Japan, especially the many multi-store owners (roughly 55,000 stores nationally, all three chains). They pay a monthly fee plus a share of the waste they cut. First targets are Osaka owners reachable through the franchisee union and owner LINE groups.
problem: The royalty is charged on gross profit calculated as if discarded food never existed. At Seven, HQ absorbs only 15% of disposal cost and the owner absorbs 85%. So HQ's ordering AI and the field counselors (OFC) push order quantities toward what maximizes HQ's royalty, not the owner's take-home. Take a rice ball that costs ¥100 and sells at ¥160. With a 60% royalty on the ¥60 gross profit, the owner keeps about ¥24 when it sells and loses about ¥85 when it is binned. HQ makes about ¥36 on a sale and loses about ¥15 on a discard. The owner-optimal stocking level is far lower than HQ's, and no owner has a tool that shows this. Markdowns would close much of the gap, but staff are reluctant to apply stickers and owners fear the OFC's disapproval.
solution: The owner photographs the daily disposal-scan printout and the hourly sales sheet, or forwards a CSV. The tool never touches HQ systems. Each afternoon it returns a per-category order guide such as 'cut salmon onigiri by 4 at the 16:00 delivery, add 2 tempura udon'. It also gives a markdown clock, for example 'sticker at 20:40, deeper cut at 23:10', calculated from the owner's actual royalty tier, disposal share and sell-through curve. A one-page 'why I ordered less' printout gives the owner data to answer the OFC. Phase two adds an owner-side dashboard showing true hourly wage after royalty and self-labor. It also adds a contract-exit and renegotiation calculator, and anonymized peer benchmarks that owners can use collectively.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises to ¥1,231 on 1 October 2026, up ¥54 after ¥63 last year. Labor is the biggest cost, and waste is the last controllable line item. HQ-side AI ordering is now the default, so owners increasingly follow machine suggestions they cannot audit. Chains have grudgingly allowed markdowns since the JFTC's 2009 order against Seven-Eleven Japan for obstructing them, but owners still lack tools to price them properly.
revenue_model: ¥4,900 per store per month, plus 20-25% of documented waste reduction for the first 12 months. If a store saves ¥80-100k a month, the fee is easy to justify. Multi-store owners get a bundle. Later revenue comes from an owner-benchmark subscription and referrals to specialist franchise lawyers and accountants.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is not a shared problem between HQ and owner. The contract makes it the owner's problem alone, while HQ's revenue is almost indifferent to it. The newsvendor critical ratio for the owner is about 22%, versus about 70% for HQ. Every 'AI ordering recommendation' is optimized for the wrong party's payoff. Nobody built the owner's-side calculator because owners fear retaliation and VCs assume HQ systems are neutral.
first_30_days: Use my three stores as the lab. Photograph two weeks of disposal sheets and hourly sales, then back-test the newsvendor plus markdown model against what actually happened. Build a LINE bot with photo OCR and a spreadsheet engine. Recruit 10 owners from union chat groups and Facebook franchisee groups. Run a free 4-week gain-share pilot with a signed baseline for each store. Publish a one-page 'royalty asymmetry' explainer that spreads owner-to-owner. Convert the pilot to paid at week 5.

title: RouteRx: Pharmacy Delivery on Co-op Fuel Routes
one_liner: Piggyback prescription and essentials delivery onto the propane, fuel and feed routes that already pass most rural households, so surviving independent pharmacies can serve people the chains just abandoned.
customer: Independent rural pharmacies (per-delivery fee), Medicare Advantage and Part D plans and rural health clinics (per-member adherence and wellness-check fee), and the co-op energy department, which keeps a share of route revenue.
problem: Rite Aid is gone, Walgreens is closing about 1,200 stores through 2027, and more than 2,000 US pharmacies closed in 2025 alone. Rural residents, especially older ones on propane and well water, are hours from a counter. Standalone courier delivery in a county of 12,000 people costs $15 to $30 a drop in deadhead miles. Independents cannot afford it, and plans cannot buy adherence in places with no last mile.
solution: The co-op's energy drivers already pass nearly every farmstead and acreage in a 25-mile radius on weekly or monthly cycles. They know the gate codes, where the dog is, and which customers live alone. Add a locked, tamper-evident tote and a driver app with signature capture and temperature logging. A partner pharmacy dispenses, and the driver acts as its contracted courier under existing Iowa delivery rules, with no controlled substances at first. Add optional 'no-heat and welfare check' notes that flag when a propane customer looks unwell, triggering a call to family or the clinic.
why_now: The 2025 to 2026 pharmacy shakeout has left rural pharmacy deserts, and Drug Channels' August 2026 analysis describes a K-shaped market of urban consolidation and rural lost access. Payers are looking for adherence and social-needs benefits. Co-op energy departments are under margin pressure and need new route revenue.
revenue_model: $5 to $9 per delivery from pharmacies. Medicare Advantage and Part D plan per-member-per-month adherence and check-in fees. The co-op takes a route revenue share of roughly 30%. Optional expansion to labs, groceries and parcels.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in rural health is not delivery technology but route density that is already paid for. A propane bobtail passing a home every three weeks has a near-zero marginal stop cost, and it carries something no courier startup has, which is trust from decades of showing up.
first_30_days: Sign one co-op with an LP fleet and one independent pharmacy in an adjacent town that just lost a competitor. Get a written read from the Iowa Board of Pharmacy and the co-op's insurer. Run a 20-household pilot with tamper-evident bags and an off-the-shelf delivery app. Record cost per stop and refill adherence to pitch a regional Medicare Advantage plan.

title: Cancellation Compliance for Regional Gym Chains
one_liner: A drop-in cancel-and-freeze portal that meets each state's auto-renewal rules and writes straight into the billing system.
customer: Regional gym and studio chains with 10-300 locations still using in-person or certified-mail cancellations, and franchisors.
problem: The FTC's national click-to-cancel rule was vacated in July 2025, but enforcement continues (the FTC sued Fitness International/LA Fitness over cancellation hurdles), state auto-renewal laws demand online cancellation if you joined online, and New York City's own click-to-cancel rule takes effect October 1, 2026. Chains run legacy contracts and billing where cancellation is manual, so exposure is AG settlements and class actions.
solution: A white-labeled 'Cancel, Pause, Downgrade' portal with a jurisdiction rules engine (notice periods, save-offer limits, refund proration, confirmations) that writes to the chain's billing platform through API or RPA, with audit logs and legally bounded retention offers.
why_now: NYC's October 1, 2026 deadline, the FTC's restart of subscription rulemaking, and active state AG scrutiny create a dated trigger with budget.
revenue_model: $150-400 per location per month plus $2k setup; share of saved revenue on approved retention flows.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance opens the door, retention pays for it: a compliant flow with legally allowed save offers often lifts net retention versus the friction chains use today, so the CFO buys it. The moat is the multi-state rules matrix plus billing-system integrations.
first_30_days: Build a rules matrix for 10 states plus NYC with a consumer-protection lawyer, sell a $1k mystery-shop 'compliance scan' of each chain's cancellation flow to 20 regional chains, and convert two into design partners.

title: Critical-Error Benchmark for Legal Transcription AI
one_liner: An independent, reporter-built test suite that scores transcription AI on the errors that lose cases, such as dropped negatives, swapped numbers, wrong speaker and uh-huh versus huh-uh. Court and law-firm buyers pay for procurement reports, and vendors pay for certification.
customer: State court administrative offices and county courts running digital-recording or AI pilots. Large law firm innovation and procurement teams. Insurer litigation-management groups. The AI transcription vendors themselves, who buy a certification badge.
problem: Every vendor claims 95-99% accuracy, measured as word error rate on clean audio. That metric treats 'I did not see him' becoming 'I did see him' as one wrong word in six, no worse than a dropped 'the.' Reporters know the real failure points: negations, numbers (fifteen versus fifty), proper names, speaker attribution in crosstalk, uh-huh versus huh-uh, soft-spoken witnesses, and interpreted testimony. Court procurement officers and firm buyers have no independent comparison, so RFPs copy vendor claims.
solution: Build a hidden test set from staged mock depositions and hearings. Working reporters play scripted witnesses and attorneys, recorded in courtroom reverb, on Zoom, with masks, accents and interpreters. Each recording has certified steno ground truth and annotated critical-error spans. Publish a Critical Error Rate per hour with per-category scores. Release a free public subset and leaderboard for credibility. Charge for private bake-offs on a buyer's own audio, graded by reporters. Sell annual certification with re-testing whenever a vendor updates its model.
why_now: Shortages are pushing courts to adopt digital and AI reporting, and Texas, North Dakota and California have all moved on it in different ways. The federal proposal for new Rule 707 signals that courts want reliability standards for machine output. Vendors are consolidating (Verbit owns Veritext). State court technology offices are writing RFPs now with no independent yardstick.
revenue_model: $15,000-$40,000 per court or firm procurement evaluation. $25,000-$75,000 per year per vendor for certification and re-testing. $3,000-$8,000 per year for benchmark subscription reports to firms and insurers. Licensing test sets to vendors under strict separation from the certification arm.
non_obvious_insight: Accuracy is measured by the people selling it. The profession that produces legal ground truth for a living is the natural auditor. A dropped 'not' is the error class that ends careers in this field, and word error rate hides it as noise.
first_30_days: Hire 8 working reporters at $75-$100 per hour for weekend sessions. Produce 20 hours of staged audio and run 6 vendors. Publish a free 'Negation Error Report' that reporter associations will share. Email 15 state court technology officers and the National Center for State Courts. Offer each vendor a free re-test to start certification conversations.

title: Smoke-and-Heat Escape Benefit for Remote Teams
angle: Pairing 1: Climate adaptation x Travel/hospitality (remote-work travel)
one_liner: An employer-paid standby membership that, when smoke, heat-dome or evacuation triggers hit, moves remote employees within hours into pre-contracted hotel rooms with a tested desk and wifi outside the hazard zone.
customer: Heads of People or Business Continuity at remote-first companies of 150-2,000 staff (dev tools, fintech, SaaS, online education) where at least 15% of employees live in US West, Southwest, Gulf Coast or Canadian wildfire belts. They have no office to fall back on and a duty-of-care gap.
problem: When AQI hits 300, a heat dome coincides with a failed AC, or an evacuation order lands, remote employees improvise: sold-out hotels, price gouging, expense fights, lost work days. Corporate travel tools are built for planned trips, and consumer OTAs cannot guarantee inventory in an evacuation. Employers carry the productivity loss and the liability but have no product to buy.
solution: Employer buys standby access. Opted-in employees are monitored by home ZIP against public feeds (AQI forecasts, NWS extreme-heat warnings, evacuation zones, NHC cone). On a trigger the employee gets a one-tap offer: a confirmed room or extended-stay unit 100-400 miles away in a cleaner or cooler basin, at a pre-contracted rate, wifi speed-tested, pet and kid rules known, paid by virtual card. Hotels earn a small standby retainer on rooms held for trigger nights. Start with mid-tier and economy properties.
why_now: The 2026 travel market is K-shaped: mid and lower hotel tiers are pressured and booking windows shrank to about 33 days, so hoteliers will trade a discount for forward-committed revenue. Summer 2026 brought the hottest US July on record and a deadly European heatwave, making hazard seasons an HR planning assumption. Remote work is now normal enough that 'work from anywhere' relocation is a benefit line item, not an emergency.
revenue_model: $6-9 per employee per month for standby access and trigger monitoring, plus room nights at the contracted rate with about 12% platform margin. A 2,000-person employer is roughly $140-215K ARR before usage. Hotel-side retainer is funded out of the margin, not charged to hotels.
non_obvious_insight: Remote work turns evacuation from an unpredictable personal disaster into a budgetable HR benefit, because the worker's office travels with them. Smoke plumes and heat domes are regional and forecastable 24-72 hours out, so rooms can be bought as standby capacity instead of emergency spot inventory. Nobody sells this because benefits vendors do not touch hotel inventory and travel vendors do not monitor hazards.
first_30_days: Pick two hazard basins: Pacific Northwest/Northern California smoke, and Phoenix/Las Vegas heat. Handshake standby rates with 15-20 mid-tier hotels and extended-stay properties on both sides of each escape corridor. Recruit 3 remote-first startups through founder and People-ops Slack communities on a pay-per-activation pilot ($0 subscription for 60 days) with 30-50 opted-in employees each. Run it manually with a Slack bot, a spreadsheet and virtual cards. Publish a 'cost of a smoke day' calculator to generate leads.

title: Volumetric Concert Replays for Small Venues
one_liner: A multi-camera Gaussian-splat capture rig that lets attendees of 200-2,000 capacity shows buy a free-viewpoint replay of their favorite songs.
customer: Independent venues, promoters and mid-tier touring acts, with ticket-holders as end buyers at $5-15 per replay.
problem: Small acts earn only from tickets and merch, and concert film needs a crew. Sphere grossed $420.5M in 2024 but is for superstars. Fans want to relive the night from where they stood, and no affordable product delivers it.
solution: A 12-24 camera synced rig hung on lighting truss, cloud splat processing, and a phone and headset web viewer. Attendees unlock replays via a ticket QR code. Start with one or two songs with static cameras and add motion later, with revenue shared with the venue and artist.
why_now: 4D Gaussian splatting hit practical quality and cost in 2025-26, web viewers are mature, and headsets are common enough to matter.
revenue_model: $2-5k capture fee per show or free capture with 50% of replay sales, plus venue subscription for archives.
non_obvious_insight: The asset is not the film but the fan's own position. Selling 'the replay from where I stood' to the 300 people who attended targets a captive small market with high willingness to pay.
first_30_days: Build a 12-camera rig for about $8k. Capture 3 local shows in exchange for rights. Test QR-code replay sales at the merch table and measure conversion.

title: Closing-Time Recovery for Shutting Small Businesses
one_liner: A contingency-fee agent that finds and collects the money owners forget when they close: tariff refunds, overpaid taxes, insurance returns, deposits and vendor credits.
customer: Owners of small businesses closing or filing Chapter 7 or Subchapter V (restaurants, boutique importers, e-commerce brands, agencies), plus trustees and wind-down lawyers who will not chase small assets.
problem: Exhausted owners walk away from uncollected money. Customs owes about $166B in IEEPA tariff refunds to roughly 330,000 importers after the Supreme Court struck the tariffs down on February 20, 2026, with refunds running through CBP's CAPE portal and protest windows expiring on a rolling basis. Beyond tariffs, there are overpaid sales and payroll taxes, unearned insurance premium, utility and landlord deposits, vendor credits, customer deposits, workers' comp dividends and unclaimed property. Trustees often skip small claims because the cost outweighs the return.
solution: Run a standard 40-item recovery checklist automatically: pull entry data through a licensed customs-broker partner with a power of attorney, search unclaimed property, send insurer audit and refund requests, and file claims with a partner wind-down attorney. Find leads from PACER filings, state dissolution records, lien releases, landlords and accountants. Take 20-30% of recovered funds and pay nothing if nothing is found.
why_now: Tariff refunds are moving but the deadlines to claim them are rolling off. Higher rates, the energy shock and squeezed lower-income consumers are pushing more small businesses to close. Contingency-fee legal and customs partners are available and CBP now has a digital claim channel.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered amounts, with typical finds of $8-40k per closing business. Referral fees from trustees and lawyers.
non_obvious_insight: The biggest asset in a dying small business is often not equipment but claims against governments and vendors the owner does not know exist. A closing owner has no bandwidth, so willingness to hand over a percentage is high, and the funnel widens in every downturn.
first_30_days: Partner with one wind-down attorney and one customs broker. Pull recent Chapter 7 and Subchapter V filings of importers and closed restaurants and send 300 letters offering no-win-no-fee reviews. Target 10 signed engagements and use the first recoveries as case studies.

title: Cash Caregiver Rails: Deductible, Reimbursable, Legal
one_liner: Payroll plus clinician plan-of-care paperwork that turns cash-paid family and neighbor caregivers into tax-deductible, insurance-reimbursable, workers'-comp-covered employment.
customer: Adult children and spouses who pay $15-30 an hour in cash to informal home aides for a parent with dementia, frailty or serious illness. The households spend $20-60K a year, and some have long-term care insurance.
problem: A large slice of elder home care runs on cash, word of mouth and no paperwork. Families lose tax deductions and long-term care insurance benefits that require documentation. They carry unlimited liability for injuries in their home and owe unpaid household-employer taxes. The aide has no wage record, comp cover, or path to benefits. Agencies solve this at $35+ an hour, which many families can't afford.
solution: An employer-of-record service for family-hired caregivers. It provides payroll, tax filing (household employer) and workers' comp or injury cover. A telehealth nurse practitioner certifies chronic illness and writes a plan of care, which are the tax and long-term care insurance requirements for 'qualified long-term care services'. A claims-ready packet is generated for long-term care insurers and the family's tax preparer, and a shift-check-in log is kept. Optional backup-aide pool for absences.
why_now: Boomers are in their 80s. Agency costs keep rising, and 2025-26 Medicaid funding cuts push more families toward informal care. Telehealth nurse practitioner visits make chronic-illness certification cheap. Household payroll rails and workers'-comp programs for single-worker households are now easy to embed through APIs.
revenue_model: $99-149 per household per month platform fee plus payroll processing. An annual $150-250 clinician certification fee. An insurer-paid fee, or employer benefit contract, for claim-ready documentation that reduces fraud and denial disputes. Backup-aide shifts at a margin.
non_obvious_insight: Families don't pay for compliance. They pay when the paperwork unlocks money that is currently being left on the table: deductions and insurance benefits that are only available to a documented, plan-of-care relationship. The clinician certification is the wedge, and payroll is just plumbing. Selling it as 'get reimbursed' rather than 'stay legal' changes conversion completely. It also builds a data asset that insurers will pay for.
first_30_days: Partner with a tax-preparer network or elder-law attorneys and geriatric care managers who see cash caregivers daily. Contract a telehealth nurse practitioner group for plan-of-care certifications. Use an existing household payroll provider under white-label. Sign 15 families at $99/month with a money-back guarantee tied to documented reimbursements. Measure recovered dollars per household as the headline metric.
